summary: Refined the @joint_apply_order question because its first hypothesis was too loose to test. Re-reading the joint and auto-leave path shows the panic should be unreachable under in-order application: the leave-joint entry is proposed by appliedTo as soon as the joint change is applied at the leader, sits at a later index than that change, and any subsequent joint-entering change is appended only after it, so a node that applies its own log in order is non-joint again when it reaches the new change; the leader-side rewrite in stepLeader (which replaces a joint-entering change with a normal entry whenever the leader's tracker is joint) keeps such an entry out of the log in the first place. That narrows the possibilities to two testable ones, which the investigation now records as its hypothesis and discriminator: either the harness applied changes out of the order its own log provided (a harness defect, plausible given the panic appeared in a model that skipped a node's whole apply step), or a permitted history exists in which the leave entry never precedes the new joint change at some node - a leader that never applied the joint change while leading so appliedTo never proposed the leave, a leadership change after which no one pursues it, or entries from different terms the application may legitimately see in an order the contract does not require. The discriminator is now a deterministic prefix instead of more fuzzing: reproduce the panic and print the applied (index, term, type) sequence to separate out-of-order application from a missing leave; build the reachability variant by stepping down or isolating the leader before it applies the joint change so no leave is proposed, then have a new leader append a joint-entering change; and keep a control where every application stays current and should never panic. No experiment requested this turn because the deterministic prefix is not written yet.
